# Glass mirrors (tin amalgam and silvering) (`glass_mirrors`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/materials.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Metallurgy & materials (`materials`)
- Deps: needs glassmaking; helped by clear_glass, mercury_amalgam, nitric_acid
- Core idea: A flat, clear glass plate backed with bright metal gives a far better image than polished bronze. The old method: smooth a sheet of tin foil on a level stone table, flood it with mercury, slide the cleaned glass across so no air is trapped, weight it, and tilt the table over some weeks to drain the surplus; a tin amalgam layer stays on the glass. The modern method deposits real silver: a solution of silver nitrate in ammonia, mixed with a reducing sugar or tartrate, coats clean glass in minutes; a coat of varnish or copper protects it.
- Pitfalls:
  - Mercury mirror workers suffered tremor, lost teeth and early death; the method needs ventilation and is best avoided.
  - Ammonia-silver solution that is kept or allowed to dry forms a compound that explodes at a touch; mix it fresh and wash the remains away at once.
  - Any grease on the glass leaves bare patches; clean with nitric acid or lye and pure water.
  - Wavy or greenish glass gives a distorted, dark image whatever the coating.
  - Pouring molten metal on cold glass cracks it; early lead-backed mirrors were made on thin, hot, blown bulbs and are small and convex.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 6000 BC – polished obsidian mirrors at Çatalhöyük; from c. 3000 BC polished copper and bronze; egypt: from c. 2900 BC – polished copper and bronze hand mirrors; china: c. 2000 BC bronze mirrors (Qijia culture); high-tin mirrors a major craft from the Warring States to the Tang; americas: c. 1000 BC – Olmec concave mirrors of polished magnetite and ilmenite; later pyrite and obsidian; rome: 1st–3rd c. AD – small convex glass mirrors backed with lead; europe: 13th–15th c. convex lead-backed glass mirrors (Nuremberg); 1507 Venetian privilege for flat tin-amalgam mirrors (dal Gallo brothers); 1835 Liebig observes silver deposition, industrial after 1856; 1857 Foucault's silvered telescope mirror; 1930s vacuum-deposited aluminium
- Read:
  - Sabine Melchior-Bonnet, The Mirror: A History (2001)
  - Per Hadsund, The Tin-Mercury Mirror: Its Manufacturing Technique and Deterioration Processes, Studies in Conservation 38 (1993)
